name: Tretinoin protocol (tret, buffering)
lead: The tretinoin protocol, often shortened to "tret" in forums, refers to the way looksmaxxing practitioners introduce and use topical tretinoin, a prescription retinoid, typically by increasing use slowly and sometimes "buffering" it with moisturiser to reduce irritation.

Topical tretinoin is described as the most extensively studied retinoid for photoageing, and studies have run up to two years.[1] Its common adverse effects are irritation, redness, peeling and sun sensitivity.[1] Reference sources do not describe buffering or slow-ramp schedules specifically, so those practices rest on community and clinician convention rather than the sources reviewed here.

paras: Tretinoin is all-trans retinoic acid. Topical forms are used for acne and for photoaged skin.[1] Practitioners in appearance communities describe starting at low frequency, increasing gradually as the skin adapts, and applying a moisturiser before or after the product (buffering) to moderate irritation. These are descriptions of community practice, not dosing instructions.

Wikipedia reports that tretinoin may increase collagen production and that visible improvement in photoageing typically takes weeks to months.[1] Topical use commonly causes skin irritation, redness, swelling and peeling and may increase sun sensitivity.[1]

Tretinoin is contraindicated in pregnancy because of the risk of birth defects; Australia rates topical tretinoin category D.[1] The American Academy of Dermatology is quoted as saying retinoids should not be used during pregnancy.[3] Among cosmetic wrinkle treatments, tretinoin and tazarotene are described as the only topical retinoids approved for photodamage wrinkles.[2]

Tretinoin was patented in 1957 and approved for medical use in 1962; Albert Kligman and colleagues at the University of Pennsylvania developed its acne use, and the FDA approved it for acne in 1971.[1] Retin-A Micro, a microsphere gel, was approved in 1997.[1]
Controlled studies of topical tretinoin for photoageing have been published, with durations up to two years.[1] No studies were found that specifically compare buffering or slow-ramp schedules.

card.summary: Slow-ramped, moisturiser-buffered prescription retinoid use; tretinoin itself is well studied, the buffering routine is not.
card.note: Prescription retinoid; contraindicated in pregnancy; causes irritation and sun sensitivity.

quick.overview:
The tret protocol is community shorthand for easing into prescription tretinoin and cushioning it with moisturiser.

Tretinoin is the most studied topical retinoid for photoageing; no studies were found on buffering specifically.
quick.mechanism: Tretinoin acts on retinoic acid receptors in skin cells, normalising follicle keratinisation and, per reports, boosting collagen. Buffering is meant to reduce irritation, not change the mechanism.
quick.risks: Irritation, redness, peeling and sun sensitivity are common. It is contraindicated in pregnancy. It is available by prescription in many countries.
